metadata.title: It's OK to Ask for Help

sections.text: Cara, is it okay to ask for help when you need it?

Is it okay? Not only is it okay, it's great. Let's dive into a cool study that was recently published in Psychological Science. This study has a lot of moving parts so I'm not going to get into all of them but I have to say just kind of at the top that I'm loving the thoroughness and I'm loving the clarity of the writing of this research article. I feel like it's a great example of good psychological science. It's based on a really deep literature review. A lot of people that we know and love like Dunning are cited who have co-written with some of the authors. This study basically is asking the question, why do people struggle to ask for help? When people do ask for help, what is the outcome usually? They did six, I think it was six or was it eight, I think it was six different individual experiments within this larger study. Their total and the number of people overall that were involved, that participated in the study was over 2,000. They kind of looked at it from multiple perspectives. They said, first we're going to ask people to imagine a scenario and tell us what they think they would do or what they think the other person would feel or think. Then we're going to ask them about experiences that they've actually had, think back to a time when you asked for help or when somebody asked you for help and then answer all these questions. Then they actually did a more real world kind of ecological study where they said, okay, we're going to put a scenario in place. And specifically this scenario was in a public park, they asked people to go up to somebody else and be like, hey, do you mind taking a picture for me? They did a bunch of different really clean study designs where they took a portion of the people and had them be the askers and a portion of the people and have them be the non-askers and then a portion of the people and have them ask with a prompt, without a prompt. The study designs are pretty clean but they're kind of complex. What do you guys think, I mean obviously you can't answer based on every single study, but the main sort of takeaway of this was?
Asking for help is good and people are willing to give the help.
People like getting help.

Right. Yeah. So not only do people more often than not, and not even more often than not, almost all the time, especially in these low hanging fruit scenarios, do the thing that's asked of them, but they actually feel good about it after. They feel better having given help. And so what they wanted to look at were some of these kind of cognitive biases basically. They asked themselves, why are people so hesitant to ask for help? And they believe it's because people miscalibrate their expectations about other people's prosociality. That there's sort of a Western ideal that says people are only looking out for their own interest and they'd rather not help anybody and only help themselves. They also talk about something called compliance motivation. So they think that people are, when they actually do help you out, it's less because they want to because they're prosocial. And it's more literally because they feel like they have to. They feel a pull to comply with a request. But it turns out that in these different studies where either they're looking at a real world example, they're asking people for imagined examples, the helpers more often than not want to help and say that they feel good about helping. But the people who need the help more often than not judge the helpers to not want to help them and worry that the helpers won't want to help them. So this is another example of kind of, do you guys remember last week, I think it was, when I talked about a study where people were trying to calibrate how much they should talk to be likable?
Yeah.
Yeah.

And they were, again, miscalibrating. They were saying, I shouldn't talk that much. They'll like me more if I talk less. But it turns out if you talk more, people actually like you more. And so it's another one of those examples of a cognitive bias getting in the way of us engaging in social behavior and actually kind of shooting ourselves in the foot because we fear an outcome that is basically the opposite of the outcome that we'll get. If we ask for help, we'll more than likely get it, and more than likely, the person who helped us will feel good about having helped us, and it's really a win-win. Of course, they caveated at the end. We're talking about low-hanging fruit. We're not talking about massive power differentials where one person, where there's coercion and things like that. But given some of those caveats to the side, basically an outcome of every single design that they did in the study was people want to help. And they want to help because it makes them feel good. So maybe the next time you need help, if you ask, you shall receive.

Yeah, also, it works both ways, too. People often don't offer help because they are afraid that they don't understand the situation and they're basically afraid of committing a social faux pas. And so they end up not offering help, even in a situation when they probably should, because the fear─
Like a good Samaritan?

Well, because people want to help and they want to offer to help, but they're more afraid of doing something socially awkward, and so they don't. So if you just don't worry about that and just offer to help, have a much lower threshold for offering, it's like it's no big deal. If it's like, oh, I'm fine, okay, just checking but people will not do it. I was once walking down the street and there was a guy on the sidewalk who couldn't get up. He clearly could not get up on his own. And there are people walking by and other people sort of like checking him out, but nobody was saying anything or offering to help. So I just, hey, you need a hand? And he did. And then like three or four people right next to him were like, oh, let me help you, you know what I mean? But it was just, again, it's not that they weren't bad people, they just were paralyzed by fear of social faux pas. So it's kind of, it's the reverse of, I guess, of what you're saying where people might not ask for help because they're afraid that it's not socially not the right thing to do. But it is. Give help, ask for help. It's all good. Everybody likes it. Just don't let your social fears get in the way.

Don't let your social fears get in the way. And also there are ways to buffer if you are scared that you're like putting somebody out. Is there are different like strategies that you can use. You can give people outs. If you really do need help, but you also really are worried that you're going to be putting somebody out by asking for help. You can say things like, I'd really appreciate your help in this situation, but I also understand that it may be too much for you and don't worry, I'll still get it taken care of. There are ways to buffer and to negotiate the sociality of that so that you don't feel like you're being coercive. And so, yeah, it's like you see it all the time. People who get stuff in life ask for it.
Or you could do with my Italian mother does and say, don't worry about me. I'll be fine. I don't need anything. The passive guilt. They are wonderful at that.
Don't forget guys, don't forget. If you help somebody, they owe you.
Someday. You might do a favor for me, you know?
That's right.

One of those things that my dad like drilled into my head that I always hear in my head all the time was he would always say, you don't ask, you don't get. So I literally hear that in my head all the time when I'm in scenarios where I want to ask for something and I totally do get that way sometimes where I'm like, yeah.

sections.title: Bitcoin and Fedimints

sections.text: Let me ask you something, David. I have a feeling that fediments are not as tasty as they sound. Tell us about Bitcoin and fediments.
Fediments. So a fediments, it's a portmanteau, I just realized I don't think I've ever said that word out loud.
You said it right though.
Welcome to the show.

That's one of those words I've probably read like a million times. I don't think I've ever said it in conversation or ever. So a fediments, a portmanteau of a federated Chowmian mint, which basically it's a way to scale Bitcoin. There's two big problems with Bitcoin scaling to achieve its goal of being a worldwide payment settlement system that's decentralized. So one of those is that it doesn't provide very good privacy. And the other one is that custody is kind of a sticky issue. You've got people on two extremes when it comes to custody of Bitcoin. You've got people who are kind of the old school Bitcoiners who will say, not your keys, not your Bitcoin, which basically they're 100% self custody. If you're not self custodying your Bitcoin, then you're not doing it right. But there are problems with self custody, which is basically if you theoretically had your life savings in Bitcoin and you lost the key to your Bitcoin, then you lose all your life savings. It's completely irretrievable. There's no way to get back. So the other option is third party custody, which the most common form is people will have it on Coinbase or Binance and they hold the keys for you. All you need to have is your username and password. And even if you lose that, you could prove your identity to them and they could restore that for you. They could restore your account for you. The main problem with that is that you're─
Hackable.

─it's hackable. It could be part of, you got a lot of rug pools, especially in the past, you had a lot of situations where somebody created some third party custody things simply to get people to put their Bitcoin on there and then they just like walked away with it.
Outright theft.

Fedimint is an idea that they call second party custody. The basic idea of a fediment is where a small group of people could come together, they could create this fediment and it would have some of the advantages of self-custody where there would be no one point of failure where one person could get up and walk away with everything and so that also gets rid of the risk of hacking as well because you would need, well, it doesn't get rid of the risk, but it minimizes the risk of a hack because you would need consensus of a group of people that say you had five people who were, they call them the guardians of the fediment, you would need three out of those five people to do anything for anything to happen to the Bitcoin. So three out of those five people would have to all get hacked by the same person in order for somebody to be able to walk away with the Bitcoin. It's resistant to the third party custody problems of being hacked or somebody just pulling the rug under you and the other problem it can help alleviate is the privacy problem which is not really achievable on the main blockchain of Bitcoin, on the base level. If you're like a really technically savvy person you can do a lot of extra steps to make your transactions somewhat private, but it's not anything that even a moderately technically savvy person could do and there's a lot of steps that you could mess up where it would fail. So anyway, so Fediment by design is much more private, it works using kind of an old technology called eCash and using blind signatures, which I don't know if we want to get to that, that's kind of old stuff, that blind signature makes it so that once you have your Bitcoin in the Fediment any transactions you do with that are essentially anonymous and it would only be dealing with anything on the blockchain if you were to withdraw from the Fediment.

Let me see if I have my head wrapped around this the correct way. So it's a blockchain where three different people have to be hacked in order for a person to actually get their hands on the Bitcoin or on the crypto.
Yeah.
And isn't the other hard part about that that would they know who the three people are inherently by the blockchain or would that be part of the problem?

So the people who are the guardians, there could be, I think they said up to 15 and the guardians could be anonymous or they could be public people. The idea of the whole Fediment is it's supposed to be, whereas the base layer of Bitcoin is meant to be completely trustless. There's no third party involved in really any of the process of Bitcoin, it's all completely automated and that's how it's designed to be. And so this is supposed to bring a little bit of trust into it. So realistically, most of the guardians probably you would want to be a publicly known person so that people would trust you and your small group to custody their Bitcoin for them. But that person who was the guardian wouldn't know any information about the people who were participating in the Fediment and they wouldn't have any information about what Bitcoin is moving where or anything like that.

The other thing that is hitting me is that you also want those people would need to be there they would have to have a presence that isn't going to just go away suddenly. Or would those three people be picked at random when a trade is happening? Is it like permanent or random?

It's permanent. So somebody would basically create or a small group of people would basically create a Fediment. The idea is that it would be implemented on different scales, but their ideal scale that they're trying to what they're trying to do is create this for community level. It's almost comparable to like a community bank.
Oh, OK. That makes sense.

Yeah. So and the idea of having Bitcoin banks goes all the way back to 2010, basically this idea that you would have a bank that was very similar to to a regular bank, but it would be based on Bitcoin. This is one of the first attempts to actually implement that, though. As like a protocol, as opposed to being most other solutions are just a company, an app, whereas this is more of a protocol layer solution where anybody could use it. It's not like proprietary app or something.

That sounds interesting. I mean, it does sound like it solves the problem of basically having your Bitcoin stolen by someone who creates a totally temporary exchange. It does it does seem to have more more of anonymous security built into it in a sense like it does seem like it could do it. Is it something that is happening right now or is this in the works?
They're hoping to have, to be able to launch probably a prototype or maybe a beta version or something around around then. So it's not available right now, but should be available soon, hopefully.

Effects of cocoa extract and a multivitamin on cognitive function: A randomized clinical trial[5]
sections.title: Multivitamins for Memory

sections.text: On the live stream this last Friday, somebody asked us about the recent study on multivitamins and memory, which I hadn't done a deep dive on yet, and I said I would do it for the show this week. So here I am. So the study is effects of cocoa extract and a multivitamin on cognitive function, a randomized clinical trial. This essentially was studying both a multivitamin and cocoa extract individually and together versus placebo. So there were four four groups in this trial was randomized and placebo controlled and blinded. And then they followed older subjects over three years. It was a telephone evaluation, but you could do that because it was essentially just a verbal mental status exam. They asked them to do verbal tasks, naming tasks, trail making, whatever. They were these were standardized cognitive evaluations that you could be that can be scored. And then you can attach a number to it. And the bottom line is that what they found is over those three years that taking a multivitamin every day was associated with a greater improvement in performance on these cognitive tests than was placebo or the cocoa extract. The cocoa extract had zero effect, so there was no apparent benefit to that.
Multivitamin?

Now I say a greater. Yeah, I say a greater increase because everyone improved. Every group improved. And that's a well-known phenomenon. Whenever you do a study like this, it's a practice effect. The second time you do the set of standardized tests, you're going to be done. You're going to do better. The third time, you're going to do better. And then it kind of plateaus. So you can do this one of two ways. You can give the test to your subjects until they plateau and then that's their baseline. Or you just have to compare it against the placebo and then you see who improves more. Is there a difference or not? So that's what they chose to do. They did not establish, they didn't do a practice series to get them to their plateau first. So a few things to put this into perspective. First of all, this is not the first study to look at the effects, the correlation between taking a multivitamin and cognitive function in older patients or in patients in general, subjects. There's been decades of research into this with pretty mixed results. There's no consistent effect here, no huge effect here. And the general interpretation of all the research has been, yeah, there's just no, nothing that you can point to that's clearly demonstrated. The reason the results are mixed is probably because there isn't a huge effect here. But the researchers took all the previous research into consideration. They wanted to do a larger study with, that's more, that's with a longer follow-up. Most studies were only like six months or a year, so they did three years and et cetera. Basically just do a bigger, better, longer study to see if they could squeeze out a statistically significant effect that way. And they did. So what does that mean? So we need to, again, statistical significance, as I've said many, many times on this show, is not the only thing to look at when evaluating the clinical significance of a study of a medical trial. So you have to also look at the clinical significance of the difference. So what, how much of an effect size is there here? And the bottom line is that the overall effect size was fairly small. It was less than the amount that everybody improved just from the study effect. Just from the practice effect. So it was pretty small, but it was statistically significant. And then the other question is, well, what could be going on here? So first of all, this could be a spurious effect and as the researchers acknowledge, we need to do this study with more individuals and with a more diverse population and we need to gather more data to see like, is this real? And if so, what are the, what's the probable mechanism? For me, the big glaring omission in this test was that they did not test vitamin levels before doing the study. Because let's say older patients, older people do tend to have lower vitamin B12 levels, for example, cause that's a hard vitamin to absorb. You need a special molecule to bind to it. It's called intrinsic factor and then sort of usher it over the gastric membrane. So it doesn't just get passively absorbed and that can decrease as we age and people could become B12 deficient as we get older. Pretty much I check it in every single patient that I have, cause it's just that one of, it's a basic neurology lab that we do because it affects neurological functioning. And it's a pretty high incidence of B12, either insufficiency or deficiency in the population being studied here. And multivitamins typically contain B12. So how do they know they're not just treating undiagnosed B12 deficiency in this population, which has a measure, which is, has a known benefit to cognition. Has a known benefit in terms of dementia B12 deficiency contributes to dementia and can cause it by itself if it's bad enough for long enough. But so anyway, that seemed like a pretty big omission to me. And I think that definitely a follow-up study would do that because that might, treating otherwise undiagnosed deficiency could be the entire explanation here, could be the entire effect.
For the vitamin industry, isn't that also kind of their argument?

The there's an important difference though, between targeted supplementation and routine multivitamin supplementation. And there is known harm, at least correlations between routine multivitamin use and other health, negative health outcomes like heart disease.
Cause you're taking too much of something.

And I'll tell you just from again, having tested vitamin levels on hundreds and hundreds of patients of all ages, but certainly many of them older, we diagnose levels that are, that are too high as frequently as we diagnose levels that are too low. And so often I'm telling my patients, stop this, stop that, and add this, you know what I mean? I have to direct their supplementation. They're taking too much of certain things and not enough of other things. That's very, very common. So just a blanket multivitamin without any pre-testing of vitamin levels, I don't think is the right approach. I don't think the evidence supports that, but all the other evidence, if you look at it in its totality, it does support, there's a lot of instances where targeted supplementation is proven to be effective and is, is good medical management, but routine multivitamin supplementation really isn't. sections.text: Each week I come up with three science news items or facts, two real and one fictitious, and then I challenge my panel of skeptics to tell me which one is the fake.
